title: Acoustic Plasmon Resonance: Breaking the Anderson Stiffness Paradigm in Quasi-Two-Dimensional Superconducting Films
authors: V. M. Kovalev, A. V. Chaplik
abstract: Recent experiments on superconducting films have revealed an acoustic plasmon mode that depends critically on the superconducting transition, directly challenging the long-standing Anderson-Higgs paradigm regarding the stiffness of the plasma spectrum in superconductors. In this Letter, we provide a microscopic theoretical framework that explains this behavior and establishes the physical conditions under which classical Anderson-Higgs constraints are bypassed. We demonstrate that in films of finite thickness, the transverse redistribution of normal and superfluid charge densities enables a unique coupling mechanism to electromagnetic radiation - a feature fundamentally absent in the conventional Carlson-Goldman scenario. Our theory predicts an acoustic mode whose dispersion, temperature scaling, and dependence on film thickness are in remarkable agreement with recent experimental observations. By delineating the regime of this acoustic response, we reconcile the observed electromagnetic activity of collective excitations with the fundamental principles of superconductivity.
summary: The paper introduces a microscopic theory explaining an acoustic plasmon resonance observed in thin superconducting films. It shows this mode arises from the transverse redistribution of charge densities across the film thickness, bypassing limitations of older models like the Carlson-Goldman scenario. The resulting theoretical predictions for the mode's dispersion and temperature scaling align remarkably well with recent experimental findings.
main_problem: The paper addresses an observed acoustic plasmon mode in superconducting films that critically depends on the superconducting transition temperature, challenging the conventional Anderson-Higgs paradigm.
main_result: A microscopic theory was developed showing that transverse charge redistribution across finite thickness allows for a unique coupling mechanism to EM radiation, predicting an acoustic mode whose dispersion and temperature scaling match experiments.
method: The authors employed a microscopic kinetic theory approach, linearizing the kinetic equation and using Poisson's equation to derive polarization operators for normal and superfluid components.
model_or_system: The system is quasi-two-dimensional superconducting films of finite thickness (d), involving both normal and superfluid charge densities. The model incorporates effects from both clean and dirty transport regimes.
key_observables: Acoustic plasmon mode frequency ($\omega_k$), damping rate ($\Gamma$), phase velocity ($s$), and their dependence on temperature ($T$) and film thickness ($d$).
important_parameters: Superconducting gap ($\Delta$), film thickness ($d$), temperature relative to $T_c$, and the ratio of mean free path to coherence length ($l/\xi_0$).
main_assumptions: The theory assumes global charge conservation and is most accurate in the low-frequency, overdamped regime ($\omega	au \ll 1$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the temperature dependence of the normalized acoustic mode dispersion and damping rate in the dirty regime, confirming predicted scaling laws.
paper_structure: The paper builds from identifying the conflict with established theory (Anderson-Higgs) to developing a microscopic kinetic framework. It derives general dispersion relations using polarization operators, analyzes different transport limits (clean/dirty), and finally presents results matching experimental observations regarding thickness and temperature dependence.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical mechanism for observing collective excitations in superconductors that are otherwise predicted to be invisible or insensitive to superconductivity, connecting fundamental quantum many-body physics to measurable electromagnetic responses.
